record.paper_title: Open Problems on Information and Feedback Controlled Systems
record.context_brief: Implications for nano and biological systems
record.original_question: In nanotechnology devices and biological systems where one part of the system improves the performance of another part through bidirectional interaction, what concrete limitations do information-theoretic and thermodynamic bounds for feedback-controlled systems impose on the operation and achievable performance of those devices and systems?

evidence.quote: one is interested in increasing the performance of one part of the system through the bidirectional interaction of other part of the system
Finding these implications is still a very relevant open question.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a composite stochastic system consisting of two interacting subsystems X and Y evolving jointly in continuous time, where Y acts as a measurement/controller that observes X and feeds back signals that influence the dynamics of X (bidirectional interaction). Assume the joint dynamics is described by a Markov process satisfying a local detailed balance condition with respect to a thermal environment at inverse temperature β, so that the second law in the form of a generalized Jarzynski/Sagawa–Ueda relation holds:

  ⟨e^{-β(W − ΔF) − I_{XY}}⟩ = 1,

where W is the work performed on the controlled subsystem during a protocol of duration T, ΔF is the free-energy difference between initial and final equilibrium states, and I_{XY} is the (transfer/mutual) information flow from X to Y accumulated along the trajectory. Equivalently, the average extracted work satisfies

  ⟨W_ext⟩ ≤ −ΔF + k_B T · ⟨I_{XY}⟩.

Problem. Determine, in concrete and quantitative form, the limitations that the above information-theoretic and thermodynamic inequalities impose on the operation and achievable performance of feedback-controlled nano-scale devices (e.g. Maxwell-demon-like molecular machines, single-electron transistors, optically trapped colloidal particles) and biological feedback systems (e.g. molecular motors, sensory adaptation networks, biochemical signalling cascades). Specifically:

(a) Identify the optimal trade-off between the rate of information acquisition ⟨I_{XY}⟩/T and the maximum achievable power ⟨W_ext⟩/T, including the efficiency at maximum power.

(b) Characterize the protocols (measurement schemes and feedback rules) that saturate the bound and describe explicit physical realizations in nano and biological settings.

(c) Provide tight, model-independent inequalities expressing how the performance metrics (power, efficiency, precision, response time) of such bidirectionally-coupled subsystems are constrained by the mutual information rate, transfer entropy, and entropy production of the joint process.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of pinning down concrete, quantitative implications of information-thermodynamic bounds for real nano-scale and biological feedback systems remains an active research area. While general second-law-type inequalities (Sagawa–Ueda, Horowitz–Esposito, Barato–Seifert thermodynamic uncertainty relations) and case-specific analyses (Maxwell demons, sensory adaptation, kinetic proofreading) have been developed, a comprehensive characterization of achievable performance limits across nano and biological devices is not settled.

status_evidence.title: Thermodynamics of information
status_evidence.snippet: Review of information thermodynamics and Maxwell's demon, noting many open questions for biological and nanoscale feedback systems.
status_evidence.claim: General bounds exist but concrete implications for specific devices remain under active investigation.
